content: Phosphoric acids and phosphates are a diverse group of compounds derived from phosphorus oxoacids. Among these, the phosphoric acids represent the largest and most varied category. The simplest member of this group is orthophosphoric acid (commonly referred to as phosphoric acid), with the chemical formula H₃PO₄. This compound serves as the foundation for a series of related acids, including oligophosphoric acids (e.g., diphosphoric acid, H₄P₂O₇) and polyphosphoric acids, which are formed by the condensation of multiple phosphoric acid units through the elimination of water molecules. Phosphoric acid molecules can link together in various structural arrangements, such as linear chains, cyclic (ring-like) structures, or branched configurations. These structures can form salts or esters known as phosphates. In its +5 oxidation state, phosphorus can be further oxidized to form paraphosphoric acid (H₅PO₅). Additionally, oxygen atoms in phosphoric acids can sometimes be replaced by sulfur atoms, resulting in thiophosphoric acids. When an extra oxygen atom is added to phosphoric acid, the resulting compound is termed perphosphoric acid. Orthophosphoric acid, the simplest compound in this series, is often referred to by its IUPAC name, phosphoric acid. It contains three acidic hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen, which can dissociate as H⁺ ions (protons) to varying degrees. The complete loss of all three protons results in the formation of the orthophosphate ion (PO₄³⁻). Orthophosphoric acid can undergo up to three dissociation steps, each characterized by a specific acid dissociation constant (Ka). These dissociation constants are often expressed as pKa values. Conversely, the orthophosphate ion can act as a base, with corresponding basicity constants (Kb) and pKb values. Oligophosphoric acids, such as diphosphoric acid (H₄P₂O₇) and tripolyphosphoric acid (H₅P₃O₁₀), are formed by the condensation of two or more orthophosphoric acid molecules. This process involves the elimination of water molecules and can continue to produce higher-order polyphosphoric acids, such as tetrapolyphosphoric acid (H₆P₄O₁₃). The backbone of these molecules consists of alternating phosphorus and oxygen atoms covalently bonded together. The naming convention for these acids follows a pattern based on the number of phosphorus atoms, such as di-, tri-, tetra-, and so on. Oligophosphates, the salts or esters of oligophosphoric acids, can lose multiple protons to form anions such as pyrophosphate or tripolyphosphate. These compounds are commonly used in detergents and other industrial applications. For example, sodium tripolyphosphate is a widely used cleaning agent. In biochemistry, phosphate esters play critical roles in metabolism, as seen in molecules like adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Polyphosphoric acids are large polymers consisting of numerous phosphoric acid units linked in a linear arrangement. These molecules can have dozens of such units, with a general formula of HO(PO₂OH)ₓH, where x represents the number of phosphoric units. The phosphorus atoms in these compounds are tetrahedrally coordinated, with four oxygen atoms surrounding each phosphorus atom. As the size and complexity of polyphosphoric molecules increase, their acidic hydroxyl (-OH) groups can dissociate to form negatively charged oxygen atoms, resulting in a variety of multi-charged polyphosphate anions. The degree of dissociation depends on the pH of the solution. In aqueous solutions, polyphosphates gradually hydrolyze into smaller phosphates and eventually into orthophosphate, especially under acidic or high-temperature conditions. Cyclic phosphoric acids, also known as metaphosphoric acids, are formed when phosphoric acid units bond together in ring structures. The simplest example is trimetaphosphoric acid (H₃P₃O₉), which has a cyclic structure and one less water molecule than tripolyphosphoric acid. When these acids lose their hydrogen atoms as H⁺ ions, they form cyclic anions called metaphosphates. Sodium hexametaphosphate, for instance, is a cyclic metaphosphate used as a sequestrant and food additive. Branched polyphosphates are formed when the third hydroxyl group of an orthophosphoric acid unit participates in condensation reactions, creating branches in the polyphosphate chain. An example of a highly branched and cyclic structure is phosphoric anhydride (P₄O₁₀). Branched polyphosphoric acids are sometimes referred to as ultraphosphoric acids. Paraphosphoric acid (H₅PO₅) is produced by burning phosphorus in dry air or oxygen gas. It appears as small, snow-like crystals and can be formed by heating pyrophosphoric and phosphoric acids. This compound has phosphorus in the +5 oxidation state and exists as pentahydroxyphosphorane (P(OH)₅). Thiophosphoric acids are derivatives of phosphoric acids in which one or more oxygen atoms are replaced by sulfur atoms. Examples include monothiophosphoric acid (H₃PO₃S) and dithiophosphoric acid (H₃PO₂S₂). These compounds are used in various industrial and agricultural applications. Perphosphoric acids contain one more oxygen atom than their corresponding phosphoric acids. For example, permophosphoric acid (H₃PO₅) is formed by treating pyrophosphoric acid with an excess of hydrogen peroxide. This compound is a triprotic acid, capable of losing three protons to form the perphosphate ion (PO₅³⁻). Superphosphoric acid is a mixture of orthophosphoric and polyphosphoric acids, with a concentration range of 62–85% P₂O₅. It is commonly used in fertilizer production and is sometimes referred to as multiphosphoric or polyphosphoric acid. Hyperphosphoric acid, on the other hand, is a highly concentrated form of phosphoric acid, prepared by dissolving phosphorus pentoxide in water or by concentrating phosphoric acid at high temperatures. This compound is also known as oleophosphoric acid and can be used in medical applications, such as releasing CO₂ from blood. Phosphate and phosphite esters are formed when the hydroxyl groups of phosphoric or phosphorous acids react with alcohols. These esters play significant roles in biochemistry and industrial processes. For example, phosphate esters are essential in energy transfer and storage within living organisms, as seen in ATP and ADP.
